claims.claim: Slusser describes Always Coming Home as building its vision through an objective-sounding layering of one didactic essay upon another.
claims.source: George Slusser, 'Le Guin and the Future of SF Criticism', Science Fiction Studies #53 (March 1991)
claims.quote: objective-sounding layering of didactic essay upon essay
claims.page: paragraph on Always Coming Home and Number of the Beast

claims.claim: Slusser reports that Cummins's reading of Always Coming Home gave him the impression of a strong identity speaking through a controlled polyphony of fictional voices.
claims.source: George Slusser summarising Elizabeth Cummins, in Science Fiction Studies #53 (March 1991)
claims.quote: a controlled polyphony of fictional voices

claims.claim: Slusser quotes Harold Bloom's 1986 introduction calling Le Guin a superbly imaginative creator and major stylist.
claims.source: George Slusser quoting Harold Bloom's introduction to Modern Critical Views: Ursula K. Le Guin (1986), in Science Fiction Studies #53 (March 1991)
claims.quote: a superbly imaginative creator and major stylist

claims.claim: Suvin writes that Le Guin delineates ever more precisely the same object, describing her method as centripetal.
claims.source: Darko Suvin, 'Parables of De-Alienation', Science Fiction Studies #7 (November 1975), abstract as printed on the SFS page
claims.quote: she delineates ever more precisely the same object

claims.claim: Suvin characterises the Earthsea Trilogy as beautiful, polished and self-enclosed like a diamond necklace.
claims.source: Darko Suvin, 'Parables of De-Alienation', Science Fiction Studies #7 (November 1975)
claims.quote: polished, and self-enclosed like a diamond necklace

claims.claim: Suvin says the closing segment of 'The New Atlantis' is rendered all the weightier for consisting of only three sentences.
claims.source: Darko Suvin, 'Parables of De-Alienation', Science Fiction Studies #7 (November 1975)
claims.quote: all the weightier for consisting of only three sentences

claims.claim: Suvin attributes much of Le Guin's stylistic power and accessibility to a blend of nineteenth-century realism, lyric-poetic technique and the ethical abstraction of American romances.
claims.source: Darko Suvin, 'Parables of De-Alienation', Science Fiction Studies #7 (November 1975)
claims.quote: account for much of her stylistic power and accessibility

claims.claim: Judah Bierman identifies sententiae as the constant feature of Le Guin's style in The Dispossessed.
claims.source: Judah Bierman, 'Ambiguity in Utopia: The Dispossessed', Science Fiction Studies #7 (November 1975)
claims.quote: the sententiae that are her style

claims.claim: Douglas Barbour identifies the wall, introduced on the first page of The Dispossessed, as one major local image running through the novel.
claims.source: Douglas Barbour, 'Wholeness and Balance: An Addendum', Science Fiction Studies #7 (November 1975)
claims.quote: One major local image—a brilliantly ambiguous one—is the wall

claims.claim: Le Guin complains that science fiction never makes the poor and the hard-working into persons.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'American SF and the Other', Science Fiction Studies #7 (November 1975)
claims.quote: Where are the poor, the people who work hard

claims.claim: Le Guin states that in science fiction the people are not people but masses existing to be led by their superiors.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'American SF and the Other', Science Fiction Studies #7 (November 1975)
claims.quote: They are masses, existing for one purpose: to be led

claims.claim: Ian Watson reads Le Guin's phrase for the forest paths as a neural simile that supports an impression that the forest is conscious.
claims.source: Ian Watson, 'The Forest as Metaphor for Mind', Science Fiction Studies #7 (November 1975)
claims.quote: a neural simile which supports the impression
claims.page: early section on The Word for World is Forest

claims.claim: Rafail Nudelman identifies thorough iconicity as the essential structural principle of Le Guin's SF, each episode being an image of the whole.
claims.source: Rafail Nudelman, 'An Approach to the Structure of Le Guin's SF', Science Fiction Studies #7 (November 1975)

claims.claim: David Mitchell states that metaphors and similes are rare in A Wizard of Earthsea, and that this scarcity is what makes them vivid when they do appear.
claims.source: David Mitchell, "David Mitchell on Earthsea: a rival to Tolkien and George RR Martin", The Guardian, 23 October 2015
claims.quote: Metaphors and similes are scarce enough to burn vividly

claims.claim: David Mitchell states that dialogue in A Wizard of Earthsea is sparing.
claims.source: David Mitchell, "David Mitchell on Earthsea: a rival to Tolkien and George RR Martin", The Guardian, 23 October 2015

verdicts.trueWording: objective-sounding layering of didactic essay upon essay
verdicts.note: Raw Wayback capture of sluss53.htm read in full (curl, 200). Quote exact in the Tristram-Shandy sentence. Note: that sentence describes Always Coming Home and Heinlein's Number of the Beast jointly ('they'), and names two devices, the stories-within-stories profusion plus this layering; the vision Slusser calls 'increasingly subjective'. ACH is squarely one of the two referents, so every limb holds.

verdicts.trueWording: a strong sense of identity speaking through a controlled polyphony
verdicts.note: Exact on the raw page, in the paragraph contrasting Cummins with Selinger: Cummins' explication gave Slusser 'precisely the opposite feel' from Selinger's. Claim's 'strong identity' = page's 'strong sense of identity'. Subject is Coming Home. Locator correct.

verdicts.trueWording: a superbly imaginative creator and major stylist
verdicts.note: Exact, inside Slusser's quotation of Bloom's introduction to his 1986 Modern Critical Views volume on Le Guin. Both the 1986 date and 'introduction' are on the page. Minor locator drift only: the Bloom quotation sits in the second body paragraph ('Increasingly, Le Guin's work...'), not the third.

verdicts.trueWording: she delineates ever more precisely the same object
verdicts.note: Quote is exact, but only in the ABSTRACT block appended after Suvin's footnotes; grep of the whole article body (lines 1-565) finds no 'centripetal' or 'delineat' anywhere. That abstract's first paragraph speaks in issue-editorial voice ('argued abundantly in this special issue', 'no contributor attempts to integrate the Earthsea trilogy'), and is unsigned; the second paragraph is the genuine article abstract, matching Suvin's opening line. So 'Le Guin writes centripetally... delineates ever more precisely the same object' is verbatim on Suvin's SFS page but is not shown to be Suvin's own writing. Suvin co-edited the issue, so it is likely his, but the page does not say so.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: attribution to Suvin as the writer of the sentence

verdicts.trueWording: Beautiful, polished, and self-enclosed like a diamond necklace
verdicts.note: Exact in the article body, section 1 ('The Dispossessing'), applied directly to The Earthsea Trilogy. Locator says 'section on the Earthsea Trilogy'; there is no separate Earthsea section, the passage sits inside section 1, but the sentence is Suvin's own and the characterisation is exact.

verdicts.trueWording: all the weightier for consisting of only three sentences
verdicts.note: Exact in section 2, 'The New Atlantis' (NA is defined as that story earlier in the same section). Page calls it 'the Atlanteans' last question-segment - the end of their strand and of the whole NA', which supports the claim's 'closing segment'. Suvin's own body text.

verdicts.trueWording: account for much of her stylistic power and accessibility
verdicts.note: Exact in the closing section (section 3), before the footnotes. All three ingredients are on the page: '19th-Century Realism', a 'Virginia-Woolf-type adoption of some techniques of lyric poetry', and 'the ethical abstraction of American romances'. Suvin hedges - the blend 'may account for' - where the claim says 'attributes'; the hedge is a softening, not a different proposition.

verdicts.trueWording: Everywhere the sententiae that are her style prepare us
verdicts.note: Exact, in the ansible paragraph as the locator says. 'Everywhere' supports the claim's 'constant', and the page's construction is stronger still - the sententiae are her style, not merely a feature of it. Scoping to The Dispossessed holds: the essay is on TD, and later Bierman writes that TD 'is signed with the same moral sententiae'.

verdicts.trueWording: One major local image-a brilliantly ambiguous one-is the wall
verdicts.note: Exact, third paragraph as the locator says. The same sentence carries 'introduced on the first page of the novel', and the next clause supports 'running through the novel': the wall is connected to the prison image 'throughout', 'time after time'.

verdicts.trueWording: Where are the poor, the people who work hard
verdicts.note: Exact, fourth paragraph as the locator says (the social-Alien paragraph). The 'never made into persons' limb is the page's own next two sentences - it asks whether they are ever persons in SF and answers 'No.'

verdicts.trueWording: They are masses, existing for one purpose: to be led
verdicts.note: Exact, fifth paragraph as the locator says. The full sentence on the page is 'The people, in SF, are not people. They are masses, existing for one purpose: to be led by their superiors.' - every limb of the claim, including 'by their superiors', is present.

verdicts.trueWording: a neural simile which supports the impression
verdicts.note: Exact, early in the essay in the light/darkness metaphorical-structure paragraph. Le Guin's phrase is quoted there as the forest paths being 'devious as nerves', and the page continues 'the impression that the forest itself is conscious' - both limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: the essential structural principle of this SF-its thorough iconicity
verdicts.note: Exact, in the passage on the radial type of linkage as the locator says. 'this SF' is Le Guin's SF (the article's subject and title). The each-episode limb is supported on the same page: a structural analogy 'of the part (episode) to the whole', the lower narrative level being 'a similarity, an image, the isomorphic sign' of the higher.

verdicts.trueWording: Metaphors and similes are scarce enough to burn vividly
verdicts.note: Live Guardian URL fetched raw with a browser user agent (200, full body text). Exact in the style-and-voice stretch. The page continues 'when they do appear', and the 'scarce enough to burn vividly' construction makes the scarcity the cause, as the claim says. Byline David Mitchell, Fri 23 Oct 2015, matching the citation.

Exact, same sentence as index 414, in the style-and-voice stretch of the same Guardian piece. Subject is A Wizard of Earthsea throughout that paragraph, and the surrounding sentences corroborate (accents 'referred to but not reproduced', no wide variations of tone or register).
